evidence: Section 4.1 defines each input type with clear linguistic motivation
Figure 4 shows how these inputs are extracted from dependency trees
The inputs align with prior work on factuality (Saurí 2008, de Marneffe et al. 2012)

strengths.title: Better event detection performance than prior work
strengths.description: The paper achieves F1=84.68% on event detection, which exceeds Chambers (2013) baseline (F1=80.30%), suggesting that the basic factor extraction pipeline is reasonably effective.
evidence: Table 3: Event detection F1=84.68% vs Chambers (2013) F1=80.30%
Section 5.2: 'We get a better performance on event detection task (F1=84.68) than Chambers (2013) (F1=80.30)'

concerns.title: Marginal improvement over MaxEnt baseline on primary metric
concerns.description: The micro-averaging F1 improvement over MaxEnt is only 0.06 percentage points (61.06% vs 61.00%), which is negligible and raises questions about practical significance. While macro-averaging shows larger improvement (52.26% vs 44.87%), this metric is less commonly used and may reflect different weighting of classes.
evidence: Table 4: BiLSTM+CNN(Att) 61.06% vs MaxEnt 61.00% on micro-averaging
The improvement is within typical noise margins for neural network experiments
No confidence intervals or error bars provided to assess statistical stability
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report confidence intervals and standard deviations for all metrics. Conduct power analysis to determine whether the sample size is sufficient to detect the observed effect size. Consider reporting effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's d) alongside p-values.

concerns.title: Limited novelty in core neural architecture components
concerns.description: The paper combines BiLSTM, CNN, and attention mechanisms—all well-established techniques in NLP by 2016-2017. The novelty lies primarily in their application to event factuality identification and the engineering of structured inputs, rather than in novel architectural innovations. The contribution is incremental rather than disruptive.
evidence: BiLSTM with attention: Chen et al. (2016), Zhou et al. (2016) for sentiment classification and relation classification
CNN for NLP: Blunsom et al. (2014), Dos Santos & Gatti (2014), Johnson & Zhang (2014)
Attention mechanisms: Bahdanau et al. (2014) and subsequent work
The paper acknowledges these prior works in Section 6 but does not claim architectural novelty
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify the novelty positioning in the introduction and abstract. Emphasize the task-specific contributions (structured inputs, two-output design, handling class imbalance) rather than claiming architectural novelty. Consider positioning this as 'effective application of neural networks to event factuality identification' rather than 'novel neural network design'.

concerns.title: Sparse precedent for event factuality identification with neural networks
concerns.description: While the individual components (BiLSTM, CNN, attention) are well-established, the specific application to event factuality identification with the proposed two-step framework appears to be novel. However, the paper does not sufficiently discuss why prior neural approaches to related tasks (sentiment analysis, relation classification) were not directly applicable.
evidence: Section 6 notes: 'Currently, only a few studies focused on event factuality identification'
Prior work (Saurí 2008, de Marneffe et al. 2012) used rule-based or feature-based methods
The paper does not discuss why sentiment analysis or relation classification neural models were not adapted
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add a discussion section comparing the task-specific requirements of event factuality identification with sentiment analysis and relation classification. Explain why the two-step framework and structured inputs are necessary for this task.

concerns.title: Inconsistent and incomplete reporting of statistical significance
concerns.description: The paper reports p-values inconsistently. For example, Section 5.3 states 'p < 0.05 for BiLSTM+CNN' in one context and 'p < 0.001' in another, without clearly specifying which comparisons are being tested. Exact p-values are not provided, only threshold comparisons. No confidence intervals or effect sizes are reported.
evidence: Section 5.3: 'For BiLSTM+CNN(Att) and CNN+CNN(Att) models, we get p < 0.05' (unclear which comparison)
Section 5.3: 'The performances of both CNN+CNN (p < 0.001) and BiLSTM+CNN (p < 0.05) models are improved after using attention'
Section 5.4: 'SIP Path can greatly improve the results (p < 0.001)' (no exact p-value)
No confidence intervals, standard deviations, or effect sizes reported for any metric
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report exact p-values for all statistical tests. Clearly specify which comparisons are being tested (e.g., 'BiLSTM+CNN(Att) vs BiLSTM+CNN(Avg), two-sample two-tailed t-test, p=0.0234'). Include 95% confidence intervals and standard deviations for all reported metrics. Consider reporting effect sizes (Cohen's d or similar).

concerns.title: Single-output variant results not formally presented
concerns.description: The comparison between single-output and two-output designs is mentioned in text (Section 5.3) but the single-output variant results are not formally presented in tables. This makes it difficult to verify the claim and assess the trade-offs.
evidence: Section 5.3: 'if we concatenate fu and fcue in Equation (19)(20) into ONE vector and design only ONE output in BiLSTM+CNN(Att), we obtain good results on CT+ and Uu (F1=63.64 and 57.80), but results of CT-, PR+, PS+ are lower (F1=49.43, 33.06, 37.07)'
These results are not in any table; they appear only in the text
No statistical significance test reported for this comparison
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Create a supplementary table comparing single-output and two-output variants with all metrics. Report statistical significance tests for the differences. Discuss the trade-offs (e.g., CT+ performance decrease) more explicitly.

concerns.title: Cue detection performance is a potential bottleneck
concerns.description: Cue detection achieves F1=66.04% overall, with particularly low performance on PR cues (F1=51.36%). Since cue information is critical for factuality classification, errors in cue detection will propagate to downstream tasks. The paper does not analyze this error propagation.
evidence: Table 3: Cue detection F1=66.04% overall, with PR F1=51.36% and PS F1=63.47%
Section 4.1 and 4.3 show that cue information is used in the fcue feature representation
No error analysis provided; unclear how cue detection errors affect factuality classification accuracy
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct an error analysis showing how cue detection errors propagate to factuality classification. Consider reporting oracle performance (assuming perfect cue detection) to quantify the upper bound on factuality classification performance. Investigate whether improving cue detection would significantly improve overall performance.

concerns.title: No cross-domain evaluation or generalization analysis
concerns.description: The paper evaluates only on FactBank. There is no cross-domain evaluation (e.g., on other corpora) or analysis of generalization to different text types. This limits the applicability of the findings.
evidence: Section 5.1: 'We evaluate our models on FactBank (Saurí and Pustejovsky, 2009), which contains 3864 sentences'
No mention of evaluation on other corpora or domains
FactBank is relatively small (3864 sentences); generalization to larger or different domains is unknown
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate the model on additional corpora or datasets related to event factuality or related tasks (e.g., sentiment analysis, speculation detection). Report performance on out-of-domain test sets. Discuss domain-specific challenges and limitations.

concerns.title: Attention weights not visualized or analyzed
concerns.description: The paper claims that attention mechanisms identify salient factors (SIPs, cues) but does not visualize or analyze attention weights. It is unclear whether attention aligns with linguistically meaningful factors or learns spurious patterns.
evidence: Section 4.2 and 4.3 define attention mechanisms (Equations 15-17, 3-4)
Section 5.3 claims: 'attention is helpful to improve the results' and 'some factors (e.g., SIPs, cues, auxiliary words) in syntactic paths play the key roles'
No visualization of attention weights provided
No analysis of whether attention weights correlate with SIPs, cues, or other linguistic factors
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Visualize attention weights for representative examples. Analyze whether high attention weights correspond to SIPs, cues, or other linguistically meaningful factors. Report correlation between attention weights and linguistic annotations (if available). Provide error cases where attention weights do not align with expected factors.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter choices lack justification or ablation
concerns.description: The paper sets hyperparameters (d0=100, dp=dt=10, nc=50, α=0.25, λ, learning rate) without justification or ablation studies. The weight α=0.25 for the two-output loss appears arbitrary.
evidence: Section 5.1: 'For the event factuality identification task, we set d0 = 100, dp = dt = 10, nc = 50, α = 0.25'
No ablation studies on these hyperparameters
No justification for why α=0.25 is chosen
No discussion of hyperparameter sensitivity
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct ablation studies on key hyperparameters (d0, α, λ, learning rate). Report performance as a function of these parameters. Justify the chosen values based on validation performance or prior work. Discuss sensitivity to hyperparameter choices.

concerns.title: Low performance on Uu events with embedded sources
concerns.description: The model achieves F1=26.26% on Uu events with embedded sources, which is substantially lower than on AUTHOR sources (F1=65.90%). This suggests the model struggles with complex nested structures, but the paper does not analyze this failure mode.
evidence: Table 4: BiLSTM+CNN(Att) Uu performance: AUTHOR 65.90%, Embed 26.26%
Section 5.3 acknowledges: 'However, F1 of Uu on embedded sources of BiLSTM+CNN(Att) is quite low (26.26), which is similar to other models'

Section 5.3 provides explanation: 'Uu only covers 23.99% among events with embedded sources. On the other hand, the events embedded in other sources usually have complex syntactic structures. Therefore, it is difficult to judge whether these events are Uu or Non-Uu.'
No detailed error analysis or proposed solutions
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct detailed error analysis on embedded source events. Identify systematic failure modes (e.g., long-range dependencies, complex nesting). Propose architectural modifications to handle complex nested structures (e.g., hierarchical models, graph neural networks). Report performance on subsets of embedded events by syntactic complexity.

concerns.title: SIP detection improvement is marginal and lacks statistical testing
concerns.description: The improvement in SIP detection from attention-based CNN (F1=73.42%) over feature-based methods (F1=72.56%) is only 0.86 percentage points and lacks statistical significance testing. This raises questions about whether the added complexity is justified.
evidence: Table 3: SIP F1 73.42% (attention-based CNN) vs 72.56% (Chambers 2013 features)
Section 5.2: 'Although the improvement of F1 is slight, however, we argue that one SIP can determine all the sources of events embedded in it'
No statistical significance test reported
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report statistical significance test for SIP detection improvement. Discuss whether the 0.86 percentage point improvement justifies the added model complexity. Consider whether simpler feature-based methods might be more practical.

concerns.title: Dependency parsing quality assumed but not evaluated
concerns.description: The entire framework depends on dependency parsing quality, but the paper does not evaluate parsing accuracy or analyze how parsing errors propagate to downstream tasks.
evidence: Section 4 and 4.1 define inputs based on shortest dependency paths
Section 3.2 uses dependency tree traversal for source extraction (Equation 7)
No mention of dependency parser used or its accuracy
No error analysis on parsing errors
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report the dependency parser used and its accuracy on the FactBank corpus. Conduct error analysis showing how parsing errors affect downstream performance. Consider reporting oracle performance (assuming perfect parsing) to quantify the upper bound.

concerns.title: Word2Vec embeddings are generic; domain-specific embeddings not tested
concerns.description: The paper uses generic Word2Vec embeddings without exploring domain-specific embeddings. For a task involving specialized vocabulary (factuality-related predicates and cues), domain-specific embeddings might improve performance.
evidence: Section 5.1: 'We initialize word embeddings via Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and randomly initialize all the other parameters'
No ablation studies on embedding choices
No discussion of domain-specific embeddings
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Experiment with domain-specific embeddings (e.g., trained on news or biomedical text). Compare performance with generic Word2Vec embeddings. Discuss the trade-offs between embedding quality and computational cost.

concerns.title: Heuristic for handling multiple cues lacks justification
concerns.description: When a Non-Uu event is affected by both PR and PS cues, the paper adopts 'the cue with the highest confidence score in o2' to decide modality. This heuristic is not justified and may not be optimal.
evidence: Section 5.1: 'If a Non-Uu event is affected by both PR and PS cues, we adopt the cue with the highest confidence score in o2 to decide whether the modality of the event is PR or PS'
No justification for this heuristic
No ablation study on alternative strategies (e.g., averaging, voting, learning a combination)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Justify the heuristic or explore alternative strategies for handling multiple cues. Report how often this situation occurs in the data. Conduct ablation studies on different combination strategies.

concerns.title: Pruned Sentence design lacks strong empirical justification
concerns.description: The Pruned Sentence (PSen) structure is proposed for SIP detection, but the improvement over feature-based methods is marginal (0.86 percentage points). The design choice is not strongly justified empirically.
evidence: Section 3.2 proposes PSen structure with detailed description
Table 3: SIP F1 73.42% (PSen-based CNN) vs 72.56% (Chambers 2013 features)
Section 5.2: 'Although the improvement of F1 is slight, however, we argue that one SIP can determine all the sources of events embedded in it'
No ablation study comparing PSen with original sentences
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report ablation study comparing PSen with original sentences and other pruning strategies. Analyze what information PSen preserves and what it discards. Discuss whether the added complexity of PSen is justified by the marginal improvement.

comparable_works.relevance: Foundational work on event factuality identification using rule-based methods
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Saurí proposes a rule-based top-down algorithm traversing dependency trees, achieving F1 of 73.59% (macro) and 85.45% (micro). The current paper uses neural networks instead of rules, achieving 52.26% (macro) and 61.06% (micro) on all sources. The neural approach is more flexible but achieves lower overall performance on the full task.

comparable_works.relevance: Feature-based approach to event factuality identification using MaxEnt
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: de Marneffe et al. use lexical, syntactic, and pragmatic features with MaxEnt classification. The current paper achieves nearly identical micro-averaging F1 (61.06% vs 61.00%) but better macro-averaging (52.26% vs 44.87%). The neural approach provides more balanced performance across classes.
comparable_works.source_trace: Referenced in Section 6 and used as baseline in Table 4

comparable_works.relevance: Attention-based neural models for NLP tasks (sentiment classification, relation classification)
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: These papers demonstrate the effectiveness of attention mechanisms in sequence modeling and relation classification. The current paper applies similar attention mechanisms to event factuality identification, but the task-specific contributions (structured inputs, two-output design) are novel.
comparable_works.source_trace: Referenced in Section 1 and Section 6

comparable_works.relevance: Neural approaches using shortest dependency paths for NLP tasks
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: These papers demonstrate the effectiveness of learning from shortest dependency paths using neural networks. The current paper extends this approach to event factuality identification by designing task-specific path representations (RS_Path, SIP_Path, Cue_Path).
comparable_works.source_trace: Referenced in Section 1 and Section 6

comparable_works.relevance: Feature-based event detection and SIP detection
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Chambers proposes features for event detection (F1=80.30%) and SIP detection. The current paper achieves better event detection (F1=84.68%) and comparable SIP detection (F1=73.42% vs 72.56% with Chambers features).

alternative_interpretations: The marginal improvement over MaxEnt on micro-averaging could be due to random variation rather than a genuine difference in model quality. The improvement might not be statistically significant with proper multiple comparison correction.
BiLSTM superiority over CNN could be due to factors other than bidirectional context modeling, such as higher model capacity, better optimization dynamics, or hyperparameter tuning favoring BiLSTM.

The two-output design improvement could be primarily driven by the weighted loss function (α=0.25) rather than the architectural design itself. A single-output model with different loss weighting might achieve similar performance.

Attention mechanism improvements could reflect the model's ability to learn task-specific feature combinations rather than identifying linguistically meaningful factors. Attention weights might not align with SIPs or cues.

The substantial improvements on minority classes (PR+, PS+) could be due to the two-output design and cue-based features rather than the neural architecture per se. A feature-based model with similar design might achieve comparable performance.

The low performance on embedded sources (Uu F1=26.26%) could reflect fundamental limitations of the dependency path representation rather than a model-specific issue. Alternative representations (e.g., graph neural networks) might not improve performance.

The paper's claim that 'one SIP can determine all the sources of events embedded in it' might not hold in practice; SIP detection errors could cascade and cause significant performance degradation on embedded events.
transparency_notes: The paper clearly describes the two-step framework and provides concrete examples (Figure 4) showing input construction. The methodology is generally transparent and reproducible.

However, statistical reporting is inconsistent. Exact p-values are not provided; only threshold comparisons (p < 0.05, p < 0.001) are reported. No confidence intervals or standard deviations are provided.
The single-output variant results are mentioned in text but not formally presented in tables, making it difficult to verify the claims about the two-output design.
Hyperparameter choices are reported but not justified. No ablation studies are provided for key hyperparameters (d0, α, λ, learning rate).
The paper does not discuss limitations or failure modes in detail. The low performance on embedded sources (Uu F1=26.26%) is acknowledged but not analyzed.
No code or data are mentioned as being available, which limits reproducibility.
The paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts or ethical considerations of event factuality identification systems.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper applies well-established neural network techniques (BiLSTM, CNN, attention) to event factuality identification. While the task-specific contributions (structured inputs, two-output design) are reasonable, they do not constitute significant architectural or methodological innovations. The novelty is primarily in the application domain rather than in the techniques themselves. The sparse precedent for neural approaches to event factuality identification reflects the novelty of the task application, not the novelty of the methods.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the paper demonstrated substantial improvements over MaxEnt (e.g., >5 percentage points on micro-averaging), the contribution would be more compelling despite the incremental nature of the techniques.
If the paper provided novel architectural insights (e.g., a new attention mechanism, a novel way to combine BiLSTM and CNN), the contribution would be more significant.
If the paper demonstrated strong generalization across multiple domains and datasets, the contribution would be more impactful.

If the paper provided detailed analysis of attention weights and showed that attention aligns with linguistically meaningful factors, the claim about attention identifying 'key factors' would be more credible.
If the paper included cross-domain evaluation or showed how the approach transfers to related tasks (e.g., sentiment analysis, speculation detection), the contribution would be broader.

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper makes a reasonable incremental contribution to event factuality identification by applying neural networks with structured inputs and a two-output design. The task-specific contributions (structured inputs, handling class imbalance) are sensible and validated empirically. However, the novelty is limited (well-established techniques applied to a specific task), the overall improvement over MaxEnt is marginal on the primary metric (0.06pp on micro-averaging), and there are significant methodological limitations (inconsistent statistical reporting, no cross-domain evaluation, missing ablation studies). The paper would likely be accepted at a workshop or a specialized venue, but would face challenges at a top-tier conference due to limited novelty and marginal improvements. The confidence interval reflects uncertainty about whether the marginal improvements are practically significant and whether the findings generalize beyond FactBank.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper proposes a neural network framework for event factuality identification combining BiLSTM and CNN with attention mechanisms. The work is methodologically sound but incremental rather than conceptually disruptive. The core contribution—applying hybrid BiLSTM+CNN with attention to event factuality—represents a competent engineering effort that adapts existing neural architectures to a specific NLP task. The novelty lies primarily in: (1) task decomposition via two-output design to handle class imbalance, (2) structured input representations derived from dependency paths, and (3) attention mechanism application to identify salient syntactic factors. However, these contributions are largely compositional: combining known techniques (BiLSTM, CNN, attention) in a new task domain without introducing fundamentally new conceptual frames. The paper demonstrates empirical improvements over baselines but lacks the conceptual divergence or theoretical innovation that would signal disruptive novelty. The work is situated within mainstream neural NLP methodology and does not challenge or reframe the underlying assumptions of the field.
logical_argument_graph: Event factuality identification is a linguistically-motivated NLP task requiring modeling of source, predicate, and cue information.
Traditional rule-based and feature-based methods rely on hand-crafted knowledge and annotated information.
Deep learning has demonstrated success in learning representations from sentences and syntactic paths with attention mechanisms.
A two-step framework (basic factor extraction + neural classification) can decompose the problem into manageable subtasks.
Structured input representations (RS_Path, SIP_Path, Cue_Path, Auxiliary Words) derived from dependency trees encode linguistic structure.
BiLSTM can model bidirectional context in syntactic paths; CNN can learn from auxiliary word collections.
Attention mechanism can identify salient factors (SIPs, cues) in syntactic paths, improving interpretability.
Two-output design (Uu vs. Non-Uu classification + cue-based factuality) can address class imbalance by separating concerns.
Empirical validation on FactBank shows improvements over rule-based and feature-based baselines.
Therefore, the proposed BiLSTM+CNN(Att) framework represents an effective neural approach to event factuality identification.

concerns.title: Limited conceptual novelty; primarily compositional combination of existing techniques

evidence: BiLSTM with attention is standard in NLP (Chen et al. 2016, Zhou et al. 2016, Wang et al. 2016)

The paper does not propose new attention mechanisms, new loss functions, or new architectural paradigms
The two-output design, while effective, is a straightforward task decomposition strategy rather than a novel conceptual contribution
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Consider framing the work as an engineering contribution that effectively combines existing techniques for a specific task, rather than claiming broader novelty. Alternatively, develop a novel conceptual frame (e.g., a new perspective on how factuality relates to linguistic structure, or a new theoretical model of source-dependent semantics) that goes beyond applying existing architectures.

concerns.title: Marginal improvement over MaxEnt baseline on primary metric
concerns.description: The improvement over MaxEnt on micro-averaging F1 is only 0.06 percentage points (61.06% vs 61.00%), which is within typical noise margins and may not represent a meaningful advance. This raises questions about the practical significance of the proposed approach.
evidence: Table 4: BiLSTM+CNN(Att) Micro-A 61.06% vs MaxEnt Micro-A 61.00%
No statistical significance test reported for this comparison
The improvement is smaller than the variance typically observed in neural network training
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report confidence intervals or standard deviations across multiple runs to assess the stability of the improvement. Conduct statistical significance testing (e.g., paired t-test) to determine whether the improvement is statistically meaningful. Consider whether the added model complexity is justified by the marginal gain.

concerns.title: Inconsistent and incomplete reporting of statistical significance
concerns.description: The paper reports p-values inconsistently and incompletely. For example, Section 5.3 states 'p < 0.05 for BiLSTM+CNN' and 'p < 0.001 for CNN+CNN' for attention mechanism effectiveness, but the exact p-values are not provided, and the distinction between comparisons is unclear.

Section 5.3: 'The performances of both CNN+CNN (p < 0.001) and BiLSTM+CNN (p < 0.05) models are improved after using attention' (contradicts earlier statement)
No p-values reported for BiLSTM+CNN(Att) vs MaxEnt comparison, despite claiming superiority
No confidence intervals or standard deviations reported
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide exact p-values (not just threshold comparisons) for all statistical tests. Clearly specify which models/metrics are being compared in each test. Report confidence intervals and standard deviations across multiple runs. Use a consistent notation for statistical results.

Investigate whether applying neural methods to cue detection (similar to SIP detection) would improve overall performance. Provide error analysis showing which types of cues are most problematic.

concerns.title: Arbitrary hyperparameter choices without ablation studies

concerns.title: SIP detection improvement marginal and not statistically tested

concerns.title: Heuristic for handling multiple cues lacks justification
concerns.description: When a Non-Uu event is affected by both PR and PS cues, the model adopts 'the cue with the highest confidence score in o2'. This heuristic is mentioned but not justified or evaluated.

No analysis of how often this situation occurs
No evaluation of whether this heuristic is optimal or whether alternative strategies (e.g., averaging, voting) would perform better

Provide justification for the chosen heuristic or propose a more principled approach.

uncertainty_flags: Conceptual novelty is limited; the work primarily combines existing techniques (BiLSTM, CNN, attention) without introducing fundamentally new ideas or theoretical insights.
Practical significance of improvements is questionable: micro-averaging improvement over MaxEnt is only 0.06 percentage points, which may be within noise margins.
Statistical significance reporting is inconsistent and incomplete; exact p-values are not provided for all comparisons.
Cue detection bottleneck (F1=66.04%, especially 51.36% for PR cues) is not adequately addressed; error propagation to downstream tasks is not analyzed.
Generalization to other domains is unknown; evaluation is limited to FactBank with 5-fold cross-validation.
Attention weights are not visualized or analyzed; unclear whether attention aligns with linguistically meaningful factors.
Low performance on embedded sources (Uu F1=26.26%) suggests the model struggles with complex nested structures, but this is not thoroughly investigated.
Dependency parsing quality is assumed but not evaluated; parsing errors could cascade through the pipeline.
Hyperparameter choices (α=0.25, d0=100, etc.) appear arbitrary; no ablation studies justify these choices.
Single-output variant results are mentioned in text but not formally presented in tables, making verification difficult.
SIP detection improvement is marginal (0.86 percentage points) and not statistically tested.
Pruned Sentence (PSen) design is not thoroughly justified; improvement is marginal and alternative representations are not explored.
Multiple cue handling heuristic is mentioned but not justified or evaluated against alternatives.
alternative_interpretations: The marginal improvement over MaxEnt (0.06 percentage points on micro-averaging) could indicate that the neural approach is not substantially better, and the added complexity may not be justified. Alternatively, the improvement could be statistically significant despite being small in magnitude; proper statistical testing would clarify this.

The two-output design could be viewed as a form of multi-task learning rather than a novel architectural contribution. The improvement on minority classes could be attributed to the multi-task learning effect rather than the specific design choice.

BiLSTM's superiority over CNN could be due to factors other than bidirectional context modeling: model capacity, optimization dynamics, or hyperparameter tuning. A more controlled comparison (e.g., matching model capacity) would be needed to isolate the effect of bidirectionality.

The attention mechanism's effectiveness could be a general property of attention in sequence modeling rather than specific to this task. The paper does not provide evidence that attention is particularly suited to identifying SIPs and cues.

The low performance on embedded sources (Uu F1=26.26%) could reflect fundamental limitations of the approach (e.g., inability to model long-range dependencies) rather than just the complexity of nested structures. Alternative architectures (e.g., Transformers, graph neural networks) might perform better.

The paper's framing of the contribution as 'novel' could be overstated. The work is primarily an application of existing techniques to a specific task, which is valuable but not conceptually disruptive.
transparency_notes: This review is conducted from a disruptive-thinking novelty lens, which prioritizes identification of conceptually novel contributions that diverge from mainstream approaches. The paper is evaluated against this standard, and the limited conceptual novelty is a significant concern from this perspective.

The review acknowledges that the paper makes solid engineering contributions (task decomposition, structured input representations, comprehensive evaluation) that are valuable even if not conceptually disruptive. However, the disruptive-thinking lens emphasizes the lack of new conceptual frames.

The review treats sparse precedent as a potential innovation signal (per creativity safeguard instructions). However, in this case, the techniques used (BiLSTM, CNN, attention) have substantial precedent in the literature, so sparse precedent is not a factor.

The review separates novelty risk from methodological flaws. While the paper has methodological concerns (incomplete statistical reporting, single-corpus evaluation), these are distinct from the limited conceptual novelty.

The review acknowledges uncertainty in assessing practical significance of marginal improvements. Proper statistical testing and confidence intervals would clarify whether the improvements are meaningful.

The review notes that the paper's contributions are primarily incremental: combining existing techniques in a new task domain. This is valuable for practitioners but does not represent a disruptive innovation.

The review recognizes that the two-output design and structured input representations are thoughtful engineering choices, but these are task-specific optimizations rather than broadly applicable innovations.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper's approach (BiLSTM+CNN with attention for event factuality) has close analogs in the literature. Similar architectures have been applied to relation classification (Xu et al. 2015a,b), semantic role labeling (Roth & Lapata 2016), and sentiment classification (Chen et al. 2016, Zhou et al. 2016). The task of event factuality is relatively novel, but the methodological approach is not. Therefore, sparse precedent is not a factor; the techniques are well-established. The limited novelty is not due to sparse coverage but rather to the compositional nature of the contribution.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the paper introduced a fundamentally new neural architecture (e.g., a novel attention mechanism specifically designed for modeling source-dependent semantics), it could be considered conceptually disruptive.
If the paper provided theoretical insights into why BiLSTM is superior to CNN for syntactic paths, or developed a new theory of how neural networks learn factuality, it could be conceptually novel.
If the paper demonstrated that the approach generalizes across multiple domains and languages, it could claim broader impact and novelty.

If the paper achieved substantially larger improvements over baselines (e.g., 5-10 percentage points rather than 0.06 percentage points), the practical significance would justify the added complexity.

If the paper identified and addressed fundamental limitations of prior approaches (e.g., showing that rule-based and feature-based methods fail on a specific class of examples), it could provide new insights.

If the paper proposed a new perspective on event factuality (e.g., as a graph-based problem, as a discourse-level phenomenon, or as a pragmatic inference task), it could introduce a new conceptual frame.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper combines BiLSTM, CNN, and attention mechanisms—all well-established components. The two-output design is a straightforward task decomposition strategy. No new neural architectures or novel combinations are introduced.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper introduces structured input representations (RS_Path, SIP_Path, Cue_Path, Auxiliary Words) derived from dependency trees, which is a thoughtful engineering contribution. However, the use of dependency paths for neural models is well-established (Xu et al. 2015a,b, Roth & Lapata 2016). The two-output design addresses class imbalance, which is a known problem with known solutions.

The two-output design is a straightforward approach to class imbalance, not a novel methodological contribution
The paper does not introduce new loss functions, new training procedures, or novel regularization techniques

However, the task itself is not new; the novelty is in the application of neural methods to an existing task.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The empirical results show marginal improvements over baselines (0.06 percentage points over MaxEnt on micro-averaging). The evaluation is limited to a single corpus (FactBank) with standard cross-validation. No new datasets or benchmarks are introduced.

confidence_interval.rationale: The assessment of novelty is moderate confidence due to several factors: (1) The paper clearly lacks conceptual novelty and introduces primarily compositional combinations of existing techniques (high confidence). (2) However, the task-specific application to event factuality and the thoughtful engineering contributions (two-output design, structured inputs) have some value (moderate confidence). (3) The marginal empirical improvements and limited generalization evaluation raise questions about practical significance (moderate-to-high confidence). (4) The disruptive-thinking lens emphasizes conceptual novelty, which this paper lacks, but the paper may have value as an engineering contribution (moderate confidence). Overall, the paper is unlikely to be considered a disruptive innovation, but it may be considered a solid incremental contribution depending on the evaluation criteria and venue.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper proposes a two-step supervised framework for event factuality identification combining basic factor extraction (events, SIPs, sources, cues) with a hybrid BiLSTM+CNN neural network augmented with attention mechanisms. The core claims center on: (1) significant outperformance over rule-based and MaxEnt baselines, (2) attention mechanism effectiveness with statistical significance, (3) two-output design superiority for minority classes, (4) BiLSTM superiority over CNN for syntactic path learning, and (5) complementary signals from auxiliary words and cues. Cross-checking these claims against the manuscript evidence reveals a pattern of partially supported assertions with notable gaps in statistical rigor and practical significance. The primary claim of 'significant outperformance' is undermined by marginal micro-averaging improvement (61.06% vs 61.00%, ~0.06 percentage points) over MaxEnt, which lacks explicit statistical significance testing. Attention mechanism improvements are reported with inconsistent p-values (text states both 'p < 0.05' and 'p < 0.001' without clear distinction). The two-output design shows promise for minority classes but lacks formal statistical comparison with the single-output variant. BiLSTM superiority over CNN is modest (1.63 percentage points) and not explicitly tested for significance. The paper demonstrates reasonable empirical validation on FactBank but exhibits systematic weaknesses in statistical reporting, generalization evidence, and error analysis that limit confidence in the claimed contributions.
logical_argument_graph: Motivation: Prior rule-based and feature-based methods have limitations → Justifies neural network approach
Task decomposition: Event factuality requires extracting basic factors (events, SIPs, sources, cues) → Two-step framework
Architecture design: BiLSTM captures bidirectional context, CNN learns from auxiliary words, attention identifies salient factors → Hybrid model
Empirical validation: Model outperforms baselines on FactBank → Supports effectiveness claim
Minority class handling: Two-output design improves CT-, PR+, PS+ identification → Addresses class imbalance
Ablation analysis: Removing input components degrades performance → Validates component necessity
WEAKNESS: Marginal improvement over MaxEnt (0.06pp) not statistically tested → Undermines 'significant outperformance' claim
WEAKNESS: Attention p-values reported inconsistently → Ambiguity about statistical significance
WEAKNESS: Single-output variant results in text only, not tables → Difficult to verify two-output superiority
WEAKNESS: Cue detection bottleneck (F1=66.04%, PR=51.36%) not analyzed for error propagation → Potential cascade effects unknown

strengths.title: Comprehensive two-step framework with clear task decomposition
strengths.description: The paper presents a well-structured approach that separates basic factor extraction (events, SIPs, sources, cues) from factuality classification, making the pipeline interpretable and modular. This decomposition is linguistically motivated and allows for independent evaluation of each component.
evidence: Section 3 and 4 clearly define the two-step framework
Table 3 provides separate evaluation of basic factor extraction tasks
Figure 3 shows clear architecture with distinct input types

strengths.title: Substantial improvements on minority classes (PR+, PS+)
strengths.description: The model achieves notable F1 improvements on speculative and negative events (PR+ +6.09pp vs MaxEnt, PS+ +25.89pp vs MaxEnt), which are underrepresented in the corpus (7.57% total). This addresses a genuine challenge in event factuality identification.
evidence: Table 4: PR+ 41.83% vs MaxEnt 35.74%, PS+ 42.97% vs MaxEnt 17.08%
Section 5.3 acknowledges the challenge: 'CT-, PR+ and PS+ only cover 7.57% of all the factuality values. Hence, it is challenging to identify them'
Two-output design explicitly targets this imbalance

strengths.title: Thorough ablation analysis of input components
strengths.description: Figure 6 provides systematic ablation of input components (RS_Path, SIP_Path, Cue_Path, Auxiliary Words), demonstrating the contribution of each element. This transparency helps understand which factors drive performance.
evidence: Figure 6 shows incremental improvements from R+C → S+R+C → S+R+C+AW
Section 5.4 provides detailed analysis of each component's contribution
Examples (S6, S7) illustrate how auxiliary words capture pragmatic structures

strengths.title: Attention mechanism shows statistical significance improvements
strengths.description: The paper reports that attention improves performance with statistical significance (p < 0.05 for BiLSTM+CNN, p < 0.001 for CNN+CNN), suggesting that the mechanism effectively identifies salient factors in syntactic paths.
evidence: BiLSTM+CNN(Att) vs BiLSTM+CNN(Avg): 2.83pp improvement with p < 0.05
CNN+CNN(Att) vs CNN+CNN(Avg): 1.77pp improvement with p < 0.001
Section 5.3: 'indicating that some factors (e.g., SIPs, cues, auxiliary words) in syntactic paths play the key roles'

strengths.title: Addresses underrepresented event categories through architectural design
strengths.description: The two-output design explicitly targets the class imbalance problem by separating Uu/Non-Uu classification from cue-based factuality classification. This design choice is well-motivated and shows empirical benefits for minority classes.
evidence: Section 4.3 explains the two-output design rationale
Section 5.3 demonstrates improvements: CT- +4.46pp, PR+ +8.77pp, PS+ +5.90pp vs single-output
Weighted loss function (Equation 23) with α=0.25 balances the two tasks

strengths.title: Structured input representations derived from linguistic theory
strengths.description: The paper grounds input design in linguistic theory (RS_Path, SIP_Path, Cue_Path, Auxiliary Words), leveraging dependency parsing and syntactic structure. This principled approach is more interpretable than end-to-end learning from raw text.
evidence: Section 4.1 defines each input type with linguistic motivation
Figure 4 provides concrete example of input extraction
Inputs are derived from dependency trees, a well-established linguistic representation

concerns.title: Marginal improvement over MaxEnt baseline on primary metric
concerns.description: The micro-averaging F1 improvement over MaxEnt is only 0.06 percentage points (61.06% vs 61.00%), which is marginal and potentially within noise margins. This undermines the claim of 'significant outperformance' and raises questions about practical significance given the added model complexity.
evidence: Table 4: BiLSTM+CNN(Att) 61.06% vs MaxEnt 61.00%
Abstract claims 'significantly outperforms' but improvement is marginal
No statistical significance test reported for this primary comparison
Improvement over Rules is substantial (10.35pp), but Rules is a simpler baseline
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide explicit statistical significance test (t-test with p-value and confidence interval) for BiLSTM+CNN(Att) vs MaxEnt comparison. If not significant, revise claims to acknowledge marginal improvement and discuss whether added complexity is justified. Consider whether macro-averaging (52.26% vs 44.87%) is a more appropriate primary metric.

concerns.title: Inconsistent and incomplete statistical significance reporting
concerns.description: The paper reports p-values inconsistently and incompletely. Text mentions 'p < 0.05 for BiLSTM+CNN' twice with potentially different meanings, and actual p-values are never provided, only threshold comparisons. This makes it difficult to assess the strength of evidence.
evidence: Section 5.3: 'For BiLSTM+CNN(Att) and CNN+CNN(Att) models, we get p < 0.05'
Section 5.3: 'The performances of both CNN+CNN (p < 0.001) and BiLSTM+CNN (p < 0.05) models are improved after using attention'
Unclear whether these refer to different comparisons or are redundant statements
No actual p-values provided, only threshold comparisons
No confidence intervals provided for any performance metrics
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide exact p-values and 95% confidence intervals for all statistical comparisons. Clarify which comparisons are being tested (e.g., BiLSTM+CNN(Att) vs BiLSTM+CNN(Avg) vs CNN+CNN(Att)). Use a consistent notation and reporting format throughout the paper.

concerns.title: Cue detection bottleneck with low F1 on speculative cues
concerns.description: Cue detection achieves F1=66.04% overall, with particularly low performance on PR cues (51.36%). This bottleneck may limit downstream factuality classification, especially for speculative events. Error propagation from cue detection to factuality classification is not analyzed.
evidence: Table 3: Cue detection F1=66.04%, PR cues F1=51.36%, PS cues F1=63.47%
PR cues are critical for identifying PR+ and PR- events
No error analysis showing how cue detection errors affect downstream factuality classification
Section 5.1 states: 'If a Non-Uu event is affected by both PR and PS cues, we adopt the cue with the highest confidence score in o2', suggesting cue detection is imperfect
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct error propagation analysis: (1) measure how cue detection errors affect factuality classification accuracy, (2) compare performance on events with correctly detected vs incorrectly detected cues, (3) consider improving cue detection (e.g., with neural methods) as a potential avenue for improving overall performance.

concerns.title: Two-output design comparison lacks formal statistical testing
concerns.description: The superiority of the two-output design over the single-output variant is demonstrated only through text examples, not formal statistical comparison. Single-output results are mentioned in Section 5.3 but not presented in tables, making verification difficult.
evidence: Section 5.3: 'if we concatenate fu and fcue in Equation (19)(20) into ONE vector and design only ONE output in BiLSTM+CNN(Att), we obtain good results on CT+ and Uu (F1=63.64 and 57.80), but results of CT-, PR+, PS+ are lower (F1=49.43, 33.06, 37.07)'
Single-output results appear only in text, not in Table 4
No statistical significance test reported for this comparison
Trade-off: two-output design slightly reduces CT+ and Uu performance
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add a row to Table 4 showing single-output variant results. Provide statistical significance tests (t-tests with p-values) comparing single-output vs two-output design for each factuality category. Discuss the trade-off between minority class improvement and majority class degradation.

concerns.title: SIP detection improvement is marginal and lacks statistical validation
concerns.description: The attention-based CNN for SIP detection achieves only 0.86 percentage point improvement over feature-based methods (73.42% vs 72.56%), which is marginal and not statistically tested. The justification ('one SIP can determine all the sources') does not clearly explain why this marginal improvement is significant.
evidence: Table 3: Attention-based CNN SIP F1=73.42% vs Chambers features F1=72.56%
Improvement: 0.86 percentage points
Section 5.2: 'Although the improvement of F1 is slight, however, we argue that one SIP can determine all the sources of events embedded in it'
No statistical significance test reported
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide statistical significance test for SIP detection improvement. If not significant, consider whether the Pruned Sentence design is justified. Alternatively, analyze the types of SIPs where the neural approach outperforms feature-based methods to better understand the contribution.

concerns.title: No cross-domain evaluation or generalization evidence
concerns.description: The paper evaluates only on FactBank (3864 sentences) using 5-fold cross-validation. No cross-domain evaluation is provided to assess whether improvements generalize to other corpora or domains. This limits confidence in the practical applicability of the approach.
evidence: Section 5.1: 'We divide the corpus into 5 folds to perform 5-fold cross-validation'
No mention of evaluation on other corpora (e.g., SemEval datasets, other event factuality corpora)
FactBank is relatively small (3864 sentences, 9492 events)
No discussion of domain adaptation or transfer learning
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct cross-domain evaluation on at least one additional corpus if available. If not available, discuss the limitations of single-corpus evaluation and potential domain-specific factors that may affect generalization. Consider analyzing performance on different text genres or domains within FactBank if possible.

concerns.title: Attention mechanism effectiveness not validated through weight visualization
concerns.description: While the paper reports that attention improves performance, it does not visualize or analyze attention weights to verify that they align with linguistically meaningful factors (SIPs, cues). This limits understanding of what the attention mechanism is learning.
evidence: Equations (15)-(17) define attention mechanism
Section 5.3 reports statistical significance but no weight analysis
No visualization of attention weights or analysis of which syntactic elements receive high attention
Claim that attention identifies 'key factors (SIPs, cues)' is not directly validated
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide visualization of attention weights for representative examples. Analyze whether high-attention positions correspond to SIPs, cues, or other linguistically meaningful elements. This would strengthen the claim that attention captures meaningful factors.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter choices lack justification or ablation studies
concerns.description: Key hyperparameters (d0=100, dp=dt=10, nc=50, α=0.25, λ, learning rate) appear arbitrary with no ablation studies or justification provided. The weight parameter α=0.25 in the two-output design is particularly important but not validated.
evidence: Section 5.1: 'For the event factuality identification task, we set d0 = 100, dp = dt = 10, nc = 50, α = 0.25'
No ablation studies on these hyperparameters
No justification for why α=0.25 is chosen
No discussion of hyperparameter sensitivity
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide ablation studies on key hyperparameters, especially α (the weight for the two-output design). Show how performance varies with different values of α. Justify the choice of embedding dimensions (d0, dp, dt) and filter size (nc) based on preliminary experiments or prior work.

concerns.title: Low F1 on Uu events with embedded sources (26.26%) not adequately addressed
concerns.description: The model achieves very low F1 on Uu events with embedded sources (26.26%), which is acknowledged but not thoroughly analyzed. This suggests the model struggles with complex nested structures, a key challenge in event factuality identification.
evidence: Table 4: BiLSTM+CNN(Att) Uu F1 on embedded sources = 26.26%
Section 5.3: 'However, F1 of Uu on embedded sources of BiLSTM+CNN(Att) is quite low (26.26), which is similar to other models'
Explanation: 'Uu only covers 23.99% among events with embedded sources. On the other hand, the events embedded in other sources usually have complex syntactic structures'
No detailed error analysis or proposed solutions
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide detailed error analysis for Uu events with embedded sources. Identify common failure patterns (e.g., long-range dependencies, deeply nested structures). Propose targeted improvements (e.g., hierarchical models, longer context windows) to address this weakness.

concerns.title: No error analysis or failure case discussion
concerns.description: The paper provides no systematic error analysis or discussion of failure cases. This limits understanding of the model's limitations and potential areas for improvement.
evidence: No section dedicated to error analysis
No discussion of common failure patterns
No examples of misclassified events or analysis of why they were misclassified
Limited discussion of model limitations
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add an error analysis section that: (1) categorizes errors by type (e.g., cue detection errors, source tracking errors, syntactic complexity), (2) provides examples of misclassified events, (3) discusses which event types or structures are most challenging, (4) proposes targeted improvements.

concerns.title: Limited novelty in core neural architecture components
concerns.description: The core techniques (BiLSTM, CNN, attention mechanisms) are well-established in NLP by 2016-2017. The contribution lies primarily in their application to event factuality identification and engineering of structured inputs, which is incremental rather than conceptually novel.
evidence: BiLSTM with attention is standard in NLP (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber 1997, Bahdanau et al. 2015)
CNN for NLP is well-established (Dos Santos & Gatti 2014, Kim 2014)
Attention mechanisms are widely used (Vaswani et al. 2017)
Main novelty is in task-specific input engineering (RS_Path, SIP_Path, Cue_Path, Auxiliary Words)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify the novelty contribution more explicitly. Emphasize the task-specific input engineering and two-output design as the main contributions, rather than the neural architecture itself. Compare with other neural approaches to event factuality or related tasks to better position the work.

concerns.title: Sparse precedent for event factuality identification with neural networks
concerns.description: The paper notes that 'only a few studies focused on event factuality identification' (Section 6), suggesting sparse precedent. While this could indicate an underexplored area, it also means limited baselines for comparison and unclear whether neural approaches are appropriate for this task.
evidence: Section 6: 'Currently, only a few studies focused on event factuality identification'
Prior work: Diab et al. 2009, Prabhakaran et al. 2010, Saurí 2008, de Marneffe et al. 2012
No prior neural network approaches to event factuality identification mentioned
Limited related work on neural approaches to similar tasks
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss why neural approaches might be beneficial for event factuality identification compared to rule-based and feature-based methods. Provide more extensive related work section covering neural approaches to related tasks (e.g., sentiment analysis, negation scope detection, speculation detection).

consensus_findings: The paper proposes a two-step supervised framework combining basic factor extraction (events, SIPs, sources, cues) with a hybrid BiLSTM+CNN neural network augmented with attention mechanisms for event factuality identification.

The micro-averaging F1 improvement over MaxEnt baseline is marginal (61.06% vs 61.00%, ~0.06 percentage points), raising questions about practical significance despite claims of 'significant outperformance'.

Attention mechanism improvements are reported with statistical significance (p < 0.05 for BiLSTM+CNN, p < 0.001 for CNN+CNN), though p-values are reported inconsistently and exact values are not provided.

The two-output design demonstrates improvements on minority classes (CT- +4.46pp, PR+ +8.77pp, PS+ +5.90pp) compared to single-output variant, but this comparison lacks formal statistical testing and is presented only in text, not tables.
Cue detection achieves relatively low F1 (66.04% overall, 51.36% for PR cues), creating a potential bottleneck for downstream factuality classification, but error propagation is not analyzed.

The paper provides comprehensive ablation analysis (Figure 6) showing the contribution of each input component (RS_Path, SIP_Path, Cue_Path, Auxiliary Words), with SIP_Path providing the largest improvement (~9pp).
Performance on Uu events with embedded sources is very low (F1=26.26%), suggesting the model struggles with complex nested structures, but this failure mode is not thoroughly investigated.

The core neural architecture components (BiLSTM, CNN, attention mechanisms) are well-established in NLP; the novelty lies primarily in task-specific input engineering and the two-output design rather than architectural innovation.
Evaluation is limited to FactBank (3864 sentences) with 5-fold cross-validation; no cross-domain evaluation is provided to assess generalization to other corpora or domains.
Hyperparameter choices (d0=100, dp=dt=10, nc=50, α=0.25) appear arbitrary with no ablation studies or justification provided.

meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper presents a competent empirical study applying neural networks to event factuality identification with reasonable task decomposition and comprehensive evaluation on FactBank. However, it exhibits systematic weaknesses in statistical rigor, generalization evidence, and novelty positioning that require substantial revision before acceptance at a top-tier venue. Key decision factors: (1) The marginal improvement over MaxEnt (0.06pp micro-F1) is the critical claim, but it lacks explicit statistical significance testing. If this improvement is not statistically significant, the primary contribution claim collapses. (2) Inconsistent and incomplete p-value reporting throughout the paper undermines confidence in all statistical claims. (3) The two-output design shows promise for minority classes but lacks formal statistical comparison with the single-output variant. (4) Cue detection bottleneck (F1=51.36% for PR cues) is not analyzed for error propagation, potentially masking a fundamental limitation. (5) Evaluation is limited to a single corpus (FactBank, 3864 sentences); cross-domain evaluation would substantially strengthen the contribution. (6) The work is primarily an application of well-established techniques to a specific task, with limited conceptual novelty. RECOMMENDATION PATHWAY: If the marginal improvement over MaxEnt is statistically significant (p < 0.05), the paper makes a solid incremental contribution suitable for a specialized venue (workshop, domain-specific conference). If not statistically significant, the paper requires major revision focusing on: (a) providing exact p-values and confidence intervals for all comparisons, (b) conducting cross-domain evaluation, (c) analyzing error propagation from cue detection, (d) providing detailed error analysis and failure case discussion, (e) conducting ablation studies on hyperparameters. The paper's strengths (clear framework, comprehensive ablation, attention to minority classes) are offset by methodological weaknesses that limit confidence in the claimed contributions.
meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes a reasonable contribution to event factuality identification through careful task decomposition and attention to class imbalance. However, several critical issues require addressing: (1) STATISTICAL RIGOR: Provide exact p-values (not just thresholds) and 95% confidence intervals for all statistical comparisons, especially the primary claim of superiority over MaxEnt (currently 0.06pp without significance testing). Use consistent notation and clearly specify which comparisons are being tested. (2) GENERALIZATION: Conduct cross-domain evaluation on at least one additional corpus to demonstrate that improvements generalize beyond FactBank. If no other corpora are available, discuss domain-specific factors that may affect generalization. (3) ERROR ANALYSIS: Provide detailed error analysis showing: (a) how cue detection errors propagate to factuality classification, (b) which event types and syntactic structures cause misclassification, (c) why performance on embedded sources (Uu F1=26.26%) is so low. (4) ABLATION STUDIES: Justify hyperparameter choices (especially α=0.25 for weighted loss) through ablation studies showing performance sensitivity. (5) ATTENTION VISUALIZATION: Visualize attention weights for representative examples to validate that attention captures linguistically meaningful factors (SIPs, cues). (6) FORMAL COMPARISON: Present single-output variant results in Table 4 with statistical significance tests comparing single-output vs. two-output design. (7) NOVELTY POSITIONING: Clarify that the main novelty lies in task-specific input engineering and two-output design rather than architectural innovation. Compare with other neural approaches to related tasks (sentiment analysis, negation scope detection) to better position the work. (8) PRACTICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Discuss whether the marginal improvement over MaxEnt (0.06pp) justifies the added model complexity, or whether simpler baselines might be more practical. These revisions would substantially strengthen the paper and increase confidence in the claimed contributions.
transparency_report: Statistical significance reporting is inconsistent and incomplete throughout the paper. P-values are reported as threshold comparisons (p < 0.05, p < 0.001) without exact values. For example, Section 5.3 states 'p < 0.05 for BiLSTM+CNN' twice with potentially different meanings, creating ambiguity about which comparisons are being tested.

The primary claim of 'significant outperformance' over MaxEnt is not supported by statistical testing. The micro-averaging improvement (61.06% vs 61.00%, 0.06pp) is marginal and lacks explicit significance testing. No confidence intervals or standard deviations are provided.

Single-output variant results (mentioned in Section 5.3) are not formally presented in tables, making verification of the two-output design superiority difficult. No statistical significance tests are reported for this comparison.

Cue detection bottleneck (F1=66.04%, PR cues 51.36%) is not analyzed for error propagation to downstream tasks. The paper does not investigate how cue detection errors affect factuality classification accuracy.

Attention mechanism effectiveness is reported with statistical significance, but attention weights are not visualized or analyzed. It is unclear whether attention aligns with linguistically meaningful factors (SIPs, cues) or learns spurious patterns.

Hyperparameter choices (d0=100, dp=dt=10, nc=50, α=0.25) appear arbitrary with no ablation studies or justification provided. The weight parameter α=0.25 is particularly important for the two-output design but is not validated.
Evaluation is limited to FactBank (3864 sentences) with 5-fold cross-validation. No cross-domain evaluation is provided to assess generalization to other corpora or domains.
Low performance on Uu events with embedded sources (F1=26.26%) is acknowledged but not thoroughly analyzed. No detailed error analysis is provided to understand this failure mode.
No error analysis or failure case discussion is provided. The paper does not systematically categorize errors or discuss which event types and structures are most challenging.

Dependency parsing quality is assumed but not evaluated. The paper does not report which parser is used or its accuracy on FactBank, nor does it analyze how parsing errors propagate to downstream tasks.
Word2Vec embeddings are generic; domain-specific embeddings are not tested. The paper does not explore whether domain-specific embeddings would improve performance on factuality-related vocabulary.

The paper does not discuss inter-annotator agreement on FactBank, making it difficult to assess whether low performance on some categories (e.g., Uu with embedded sources) reflects task difficulty or model limitations.

Novelty positioning is somewhat overstated. The paper claims to propose a 'framework' for event factuality identification, but the core techniques (BiLSTM, CNN, attention) are well-established in NLP. The main novelty lies in task-specific input engineering and the two-output design, which should be more clearly communicated.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This paper proposes a two-step supervised framework for event factuality identification combining basic factor extraction (events, SIPs, sources, cues) with a hybrid BiLSTM+CNN neural network augmented with attention mechanisms. The work addresses an underexplored task with a linguistically motivated approach and demonstrates improvements over rule-based and feature-based baselines on FactBank. However, the contribution is primarily incremental, combining well-established neural techniques (BiLSTM, CNN, attention) in a new task domain. The core empirical claim—that the model 'significantly outperforms' MaxEnt baseline—is undermined by a marginal micro-averaging improvement (61.06% vs 61.00%, ~0.06 percentage points) that lacks explicit statistical significance testing. The paper exhibits systematic weaknesses in statistical rigor (inconsistent p-value reporting, missing confidence intervals), generalization evidence (single-corpus evaluation), and error analysis (no investigation of failure modes). Strengths include clear task decomposition, comprehensive ablation analysis, and effective handling of minority classes through a two-output design. The work makes a reasonable incremental contribution suitable for a specialized venue but requires substantial methodological improvements for acceptance at a top-tier conference.
strengths: Well-motivated two-step framework with clear linguistic grounding: The decomposition into basic factor extraction (events, SIPs, sources, cues) followed by neural classification is methodologically sound and interpretable, respecting linguistic structure of the task.

Comprehensive ablation analysis demonstrating component necessity: Figure 6 systematically shows the contribution of each input type (RS_Path, SIP_Path, Cue_Path, Auxiliary Words), with SIP_Path providing the largest improvement (~9pp), validating the structured input design.

Effective handling of class imbalance through two-output design: The model achieves substantial improvements on minority classes (CT- +4.46pp, PR+ +8.77pp, PS+ +5.90pp) compared to single-output variant, addressing a genuine challenge in event factuality identification.

Attention mechanism shows statistical significance improvements: Reported improvements with p < 0.05 (BiLSTM+CNN) and p < 0.001 (CNN+CNN) suggest attention effectively identifies salient factors, though exact p-values and confidence intervals are not provided.

Structured input representations leverage linguistic knowledge: RS_Path, SIP_Path, Cue_Path, and Auxiliary Words are derived from dependency trees and encode linguistic insights about factuality determinants, bridging symbolic NLP and neural methods.

Stratified performance analysis reveals failure modes: Table 4 shows performance stratification by source type (AUTHOR vs embedded), revealing that the model struggles with embedded sources (Uu F1=26.26%), which aids understanding of limitations.
Better event detection performance than prior work: Achieves F1=84.68% compared to Chambers (2013) baseline (F1=80.30%), suggesting the basic factor extraction pipeline is reasonably effective.
limitations: Marginal improvement over MaxEnt baseline on primary metric undermines 'significant outperformance' claim: Micro-averaging F1 improvement is only 0.06 percentage points (61.06% vs 61.00%), which is negligible and potentially within noise margins. No explicit statistical significance test is reported for this critical comparison, making it impossible to assess whether the improvement is statistically meaningful or due to random variation.

Inconsistent and incomplete statistical significance reporting throughout the paper: P-values are reported as threshold comparisons (p < 0.05, p < 0.001) without exact values. Section 5.3 mentions 'p < 0.05 for BiLSTM+CNN' twice with potentially different meanings, creating ambiguity about which comparisons are being tested. No confidence intervals or standard deviations are provided for any performance metrics, limiting assessment of result reliability and reproducibility.

Cue detection bottleneck (F1=66.04%, PR cues 51.36%) not analyzed for error propagation: Low cue detection performance, especially for PR cues (51.36%), creates a potential bottleneck for downstream factuality classification. However, the paper does not analyze how cue detection errors propagate to downstream tasks or measure the actual impact on overall performance. This cascading error propagation could significantly limit the model's effectiveness.

Two-output design comparison lacks formal statistical testing and formal presentation: Single-output variant results are mentioned only in text (Section 5.3), not presented in formal tables, making verification difficult. No statistical significance tests are reported for the comparison between single-output and two-output designs, despite this being a key architectural contribution. The trade-off (slight reduction in CT+ and Uu performance) is mentioned but not quantified.

No cross-domain evaluation; generalization to other corpora unknown: Evaluation is limited to FactBank (3864 sentences) with 5-fold cross-validation. No cross-domain evaluation is provided to assess whether improvements generalize to other corpora, domains, or text types. This severely limits confidence in the practical applicability of the approach beyond the specific FactBank corpus.

Attention mechanism effectiveness not validated through weight visualization or analysis: While the paper reports statistical significance improvements from attention, it does not visualize or analyze attention weights to verify that they align with linguistically meaningful factors (SIPs, cues). Without this analysis, it is unclear whether attention captures meaningful patterns or learns spurious correlations.
open_questions: Is the marginal improvement over MaxEnt (0.06pp on micro-averaging) statistically significant? The paper claims 'significant outperformance' but provides no explicit statistical test for this critical comparison. What are the exact p-value, 95% confidence interval, and effect size for the BiLSTM+CNN(Att) vs MaxEnt comparison? If the improvement is not statistically significant, how should the practical significance of the added model complexity be assessed?

How do cue detection errors propagate to downstream factuality classification? Cue detection achieves only F1=51.36% for PR cues, which are critical for identifying speculative events. What is the actual impact of these errors on factuality classification accuracy? Would improving cue detection (e.g., using neural methods) significantly improve overall performance? How much of the model's performance is limited by this bottleneck?

Does the two-output design provide statistically significant improvements over the single-output variant? Single-output results are mentioned in text but not formally presented in tables. What are the exact p-values and confidence intervals for the improvements on each factuality category? Is the trade-off (slight reduction in CT+ and Uu performance) acceptable given the improvements on minority classes?

What linguistic factors does the attention mechanism actually capture? Attention weights are not visualized or analyzed. Do high-attention positions correspond to SIPs, cues, auxiliary words, or other linguistically meaningful elements? Are there cases where attention fails to identify expected key factors? How does attention performance vary across different factuality categories?

Why does the model achieve such low F1 on Uu events with embedded sources (26.26%)? Is this due to fundamental limitations of the approach (e.g., inability to model long-range dependencies in complex nested structures), limited training data for this category, or inherent task difficulty? What specific syntactic structures or linguistic phenomena cause misclassification? Would alternative architectures (e.g., Transformers, graph neural networks) perform better on this challenging subset?

How sensitive are the results to hyperparameter choices, particularly α=0.25 for the weighted loss? No ablation studies are provided for key hyperparameters (d0, dp, dt, nc, α, λ, learning rate). How much do results vary with different values of α? Are the chosen hyperparameters optimal, or would different values substantially improve performance? How were these values selected?

Do the improvements generalize to other corpora and domains? Evaluation is limited to FactBank. How does the model perform on other event factuality corpora or related tasks (e.g., negation scope detection, speculation detection)? Are there domain-specific factors that affect performance? Would the approach work well on biomedical, social media, or other specialized text domains?

What are the most common error patterns and failure modes? The paper provides no systematic error analysis. Which event types, syntactic structures, or linguistic phenomena are most challenging? Are errors concentrated in specific factuality categories or source types? What insights from error analysis could guide future improvements?
